questions.text: Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some species can grow almost a metre in a single day. Because it regenerates from its roots after harvesting, architects increasingly treat it as a renewable alternative to timber. Its weakness has always been durability: untreated, it rots and attracts insects, so modern construction depends on careful drying and chemical protection.

zh.Bamboo is technically a grass, yet some: 竹子在學術上屬於禾草類植物，但有些品種一天之內就能長高將近一公尺。由於採收後竹子能從根部再生，建築師越來越把它視為木材的可再生替代品。它一直以來的弱點是耐久性：未經處理的竹子會腐爛並招來蟲害，因此現代營建工程仰賴細心的乾燥處理與化學防護。

questions.text: Double-entry bookkeeping, formalised by an Italian friar in the fifteenth century, records every transaction twice, once as a debit and once as a credit. The elegance of the system lies in its built-in check: if the two columns fail to balance, an error has been made somewhere. Five centuries later, the same principle still underpins global finance.

zh.Double-entry bookkeeping, formalised by: 複式簿記由一位義大利修士在十五世紀加以系統化，它把每一筆交易記錄兩次：一次記為借方，一次記為貸方。這個制度的精妙之處在於它內建的檢核機制：如果兩欄數字不平衡，就代表某處出了錯。五個世紀後，同樣的原則仍然支撐著全球金融體系。

questions.text: The human gut contains trillions of bacteria, and their combined genetic material outnumbers our own by a wide margin. Researchers once dismissed these microbes as passengers, but they now appear to influence digestion, immunity and even mood. What remains unclear is how much of this relationship we can deliberately change through diet.

zh.The human gut contains trillions of bact: 人類的腸道中有數兆個細菌，它們的遺傳物質總量遠遠超過我們自身的遺傳物質。研究人員過去把這些微生物視為無關緊要的「乘客」，但現在看來，它們會影響消化、免疫力，甚至情緒。目前仍不清楚的是，我們能在多大程度上透過飲食刻意改變這種關係。

questions.text: Volcanic eruptions can cool the planet as well as heat it. When a large eruption injects sulphur high into the atmosphere, the resulting particles reflect sunlight back into space. After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, average global temperatures fell by roughly half a degree for more than a year.

zh.Volcanic eruptions can cool the planet a: 火山爆發既能使地球升溫，也能使地球降溫。當一次大規模噴發把硫注入高層大氣時，所形成的微粒會把陽光反射回太空。1991 年皮納圖博火山爆發後，全球平均氣溫下降了大約半度，持續超過一年。

questions.text: Most people assume that memory works like a recording, faithfully storing events for later playback. In reality, each time we recall an experience we partly rebuild it, filling gaps with expectation and later knowledge. This is why confident eyewitnesses can be sincerely, and sometimes disastrously, wrong.

zh.Most people assume that memory works lik: 大多數人以為記憶就像錄影一樣，忠實地儲存事件以便日後重播。事實上，我們每次回想一段經歷時，都會部分地重建它，用預期和後來得知的資訊來填補空白。這就是為什麼充滿自信的目擊證人，可能真誠地犯錯，而且有時錯得造成災難性的後果。

questions.text: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over the past decade, with hives appearing on office roofs and hotel terraces. Cities can be surprisingly good habitats, offering a long flowering season and fewer pesticides than intensive farmland. However, ecologists warn that too many honeybees may compete with the wild pollinators that depend on the same flowers.

zh.Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly over: 過去十年來，都市養蜂迅速發展，蜂箱出現在辦公大樓屋頂和飯店露台上。城市可以是出乎意料的良好棲地，花季長，農藥也比集約化農地少。然而，生態學家警告，蜜蜂過多可能會與依賴同樣花朵的野生授粉昆蟲互相競爭。

questions.text: The printing press did not simply make books cheaper; it changed what counted as knowledge. Once identical copies could circulate across Europe, scholars could compare the same page, spot errors and build on one another’s work. Standardised texts made disagreement more precise, and precision made progress faster.

zh.The printing press did not simply make b: 印刷機不只是讓書變得更便宜；它改變了什麼才算是知識。一旦完全相同的副本能在歐洲各地流通，學者就能比對同一頁內容、找出錯誤，並在彼此的研究基礎上繼續發展。標準化的文本讓分歧變得更精確，而精確則讓進步變得更快。

questions.text: Desalination plants turn seawater into drinking water by forcing it through membranes fine enough to trap salt. The technology is reliable but energy hungry, and the concentrated brine left behind must be returned to the sea without harming marine life. For dry coastal cities, it is often an expensive insurance policy against drought.

zh.Desalination plants turn seawater into d: 海水淡化廠把海水加壓推過細密到足以攔住鹽分的薄膜，將它轉化為飲用水。這項技術可靠但耗能很高，而且留下的高濃度鹵水必須排回海中，同時不能傷害海洋生物。對乾燥的沿海城市來說，它往往是一份用來對抗乾旱的昂貴保險。

questions.text: Sleep patterns change markedly during adolescence. Teenagers’ internal clocks shift later by up to two hours, making it genuinely difficult for them to fall asleep early. Several school districts that moved their first lessons to a later start have reported better attendance, improved grades and fewer car accidents among young drivers.

zh.Sleep patterns change markedly during ad: 青春期的睡眠模式會明顯改變。青少年的生理時鐘會往後延遲多達兩小時，使他們真的很難早早入睡。幾個把第一堂課延後開始的學區表示，學生的出席率提高、成績進步，年輕駕駛發生的車禍也減少了。

questions.text: Glass is often described as a slow-moving liquid, a claim supported by the observation that old church windows are thicker at the bottom. The explanation is less exotic. Medieval glassmakers could not produce panes of even thickness, and builders usually installed the heavier edge at the base, where it was more stable.

zh.Glass is often described as a slow-movin: 玻璃常被形容為一種流動緩慢的液體，支持這個說法的觀察是：老教堂的窗戶底部比較厚。但真正的解釋並沒有那麼玄妙。中世紀的玻璃工匠無法製造出厚度均勻的玻璃板，而建築工人通常會把較重的一邊裝在底部，因為那樣比較穩固。

questions.text: Before refrigeration, salt was one of the most valuable goods in the world, because it allowed meat and fish to be preserved for months. Entire trade routes were organised around it, and several European cities grew wealthy by controlling its supply. Even the word salary is thought to be connected to payments made in salt.

zh.Before refrigeration, salt was one of th: 在冷藏技術出現之前，鹽是世界上最有價值的商品之一，因為它能讓肉類和魚類保存好幾個月。整條貿易路線都圍繞著鹽而建立，好幾個歐洲城市也因為掌控鹽的供應而致富。就連 salary（薪水）這個字，一般也認為與用鹽支付的報酬有關。

questions.text: Chameleons are famous for changing colour, but camouflage is not usually the main reason. Their skin contains layers of tiny crystals that reflect light differently as they are stretched or relaxed. Most dramatic changes occur during contests between males or during courtship, when a bright display communicates strength far more effectively than hiding would.

zh.Chameleons are famous for changing colou: 變色龍以會變色而聞名，但偽裝通常不是主要原因。牠們的皮膚含有好幾層微小的晶體，這些晶體在被拉伸或放鬆時，反射光線的方式會有所不同。最劇烈的顏色變化發生在雄性之間的競爭或求偶期間，此時鮮豔的展示比躲藏更能有效地傳達力量。

questions.text: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the moon, which stretches the oceans into two bulges on opposite sides of the planet. As the Earth rotates through these bulges, most coastlines experience two high tides each day. The sun has a smaller effect, strengthening the tides when it lines up with the moon.

zh.Tides are caused mainly by the gravitati: 潮汐主要是由月球的引力造成的，它把海洋拉伸成位於地球兩側的兩個隆起。當地球自轉經過這兩個隆起時，大多數海岸每天都會出現兩次漲潮。太陽的影響較小，但當它與月球排成一直線時，就會使潮汐增強。

questions.text: The Library of Alexandria is often imagined as destroyed in a single catastrophic fire. Historians now think its decline was gradual, the result of reduced funding, political instability and scholars leaving for other cities over several centuries. The lesson is less dramatic but perhaps more relevant: institutions of knowledge usually fade through neglect.

zh.The Library of Alexandria is often imagi: 人們常想像亞歷山大圖書館是在一場災難性的大火中毀於一旦。歷史學家現在認為，它的衰落是漸進的，是經費減少、政治動盪，以及學者在幾個世紀間陸續前往其他城市所造成的結果。這個教訓沒那麼戲劇化，但或許更切合現實：知識機構通常是因為被忽視而逐漸凋零的。

questions.text: Open-plan offices were designed to encourage collaboration, but several studies suggest they have the opposite effect. When employees moved into open spaces, face-to-face interaction often fell, while email and messaging increased. Surrounded by noise and visibility, people appear to protect their concentration by withdrawing, putting on headphones and avoiding conversation altogether.

zh.Open-plan offices were designed to encou: 開放式辦公室的設計初衷是鼓勵合作，但好幾項研究顯示，它的效果正好相反。員工搬進開放空間後，面對面的互動往往減少了，而電子郵件和訊息則增加了。被噪音和他人的目光包圍時，人們似乎會以退縮的方式來保護自己的專注力，例如戴上耳機，並完全避免交談。

questions.text: European eels begin life in the Sargasso Sea, drift thousands of kilometres to the coasts of Europe, and spend decades in rivers before returning to spawn. Remarkably, no one has ever observed eels breeding in the wild. Much of what we know about their journey has been pieced together from larvae caught at sea.

zh.European eels begin life in the Sargasso: 歐洲鰻鱺在馬尾藻海出生，漂流數千公里到達歐洲沿岸，在河川中度過數十年，然後才返回產卵。值得注意的是，從來沒有人在野外觀察到鰻魚繁殖。我們對牠們旅程的大部分了解，都是從在海上捕獲的幼體拼湊出來的。

questions.text: A carbon tax works by making polluting activities more expensive, encouraging businesses and households to find cleaner alternatives. Economists generally prefer it to detailed regulation because it lets people decide where emissions can be cut most cheaply. The political difficulty is that the costs are visible immediately, while the benefits arrive slowly.

zh.A carbon tax works by making polluting a: 碳稅的運作方式是讓污染活動的成本變高，促使企業和家庭尋找更乾淨的替代方案。經濟學家通常比較偏好碳稅而不是詳細的法規，因為它讓人們自行決定在哪裡減排成本最低。政治上的困難在於，成本馬上就看得到，而好處卻來得很慢。

questions.text: For years, researchers claimed that speaking two languages strengthened general mental control, since bilingual people constantly suppress one language while using the other. Larger and more carefully designed studies have since struggled to reproduce this advantage. Learning a language clearly has many benefits, but a sharper mind in unrelated tasks may not be one of them.

zh.For years, researchers claimed that spea: 多年來，研究人員一直聲稱說兩種語言能增強整體的心智控制力，因為雙語者在使用一種語言時，必須不斷壓抑另一種語言。但後來規模更大、設計更嚴謹的研究，都難以重現這種優勢。學習語言顯然有許多好處，但在不相關的任務上頭腦更靈活，可能並不是其中之一。

questions.text: Roman harbour walls built two thousand years ago are still standing in seawater that would destroy modern concrete within decades. Analysis has shown that the Romans mixed volcanic ash with lime, and that seawater slowly triggered the growth of new minerals inside the structure. In effect, the material became stronger with age.

zh.Roman harbour walls built two thousand y: 兩千年前建造的羅馬港口牆，至今仍矗立在海水中，而同樣的海水會在數十年內摧毀現代混凝土。分析顯示，羅馬人把火山灰和石灰混合在一起，而海水會慢慢促使結構內部生成新的礦物。實際上，這種材料會隨著時間變得更加堅固。

questions.text: Roughly a third of the food produced worldwide is never eaten. In poorer countries, most of the loss happens early, because of poor storage and transport. In wealthier countries, it happens at the end of the chain, in shops and homes, where food is thrown away simply because it looks imperfect or has passed a date label.

zh.Roughly a third of the food produced wor: 全世界生產的食物中，大約有三分之一從來沒有被吃掉。在較貧窮的國家，大部分的損失發生在早期階段，原因是儲存和運輸不良。在較富裕的國家，損失則發生在供應鏈的末端，也就是商店和家庭中，食物只因為外觀不完美或過了標示日期就被丟棄。

questions.text: The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by a French doctor who felt uncomfortable placing his ear directly on a young patient’s chest. He rolled a sheet of paper into a tube and found that he could hear the heart more clearly than ever before. His simple improvisation became the most recognisable symbol of medicine.

zh.The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by: 聽診器是在 1816 年由一位法國醫師發明的，他對於把耳朵直接貼在一位年輕病人的胸口上感到不自在。他把一張紙捲成一根管子，發現自己能比以往任何時候都更清楚地聽到心跳聲。他這個簡單的臨時發明，後來成為醫學最具代表性的象徵。

questions.text: Adding lanes to a congested road rarely reduces traffic for long. The extra space makes driving more attractive, so people who previously travelled at other times, by other routes or by public transport begin to drive instead. Within a few years, the new road is often as crowded as the old one, a pattern known as induced demand.

zh.Adding lanes to a congested road rarely: 在壅塞的道路上增加車道，很少能長期減少交通量。多出來的空間讓開車變得更有吸引力，所以原本在其他時段出行、走其他路線或搭大眾運輸的人，都開始改為開車。不出幾年，新道路往往就和舊道路一樣擁擠，這種現象稱為「誘發需求」。

questions.text: During the last ice age, sea levels were more than a hundred metres lower than today, exposing land bridges between continents. One of these connected Asia and North America, allowing people and animals to cross on foot. When the ice melted, the bridge disappeared beneath the sea, separating populations that had once been connected.

zh.During the last ice age, sea levels were: 在上一次冰河時期，海平面比現在低了一百多公尺，露出了連接各大陸的陸橋。其中一座連接了亞洲和北美洲，讓人類和動物能夠徒步穿越。當冰融化後，這座陸橋就沉入海底，把原本相連的族群分隔開來。

questions.text: Microplastics have now been found almost everywhere scientists have looked, from Arctic snow to the deepest ocean trenches and even human blood. Their effects on health remain uncertain, largely because exposure is so widespread that it is difficult to find a comparison group that has not been exposed at all.

zh.Microplastics have now been found almost: 如今，科學家幾乎在所有調查過的地方都發現了塑膠微粒，從北極的雪到最深的海溝，甚至人類的血液中都有。它們對健康的影響仍不確定，主要是因為暴露的情況太普遍，很難找到一個完全沒有接觸過的對照組。

questions.text: Just-in-time manufacturing keeps very little stock, relying on parts arriving exactly when they are needed. The approach cuts storage costs and exposes inefficiencies, which is why it spread rapidly from Japanese carmakers to industries around the world. Its weakness became obvious during recent crises, when a single delayed component could halt an entire factory.

zh.Just-in-time manufacturing keeps very li: 及時生產制幾乎不保留庫存，而是仰賴零件在需要的時候準時送達。這種做法能降低倉儲成本並暴露出效率低落的環節，這也是它從日本汽車製造商迅速擴展到全世界各行各業的原因。它的弱點在最近幾次危機中變得十分明顯：只要一個零件延誤，就可能讓整座工廠停擺。

questions.text: Birds of the same species can sing noticeably different songs depending on where they live, much as human accents vary between regions. Young birds learn their songs by listening to adults nearby, so local variations are passed down through generations. In noisy cities, some species have even begun to sing at a higher pitch.

zh.Birds of the same species can sing notic: 同一種鳥會因為居住地不同而唱出明顯不同的歌，就像人類的口音會因地區而異。幼鳥是靠聆聽附近的成鳥來學唱歌的，所以地方性的差異會一代一代傳下去。在吵雜的城市裡，有些鳥類甚至開始用更高的音調唱歌。

questions.text: Please submit your research proposal to the faculty office by Friday afternoon.

zh.Please submit your research proposal to: 請在星期五下午之前把你的研究計畫書交到學院辦公室。

questions.text: The guest lecture on marine biology will begin at half past two.

zh.The guest lecture on marine biology will: 海洋生物學的客座講座將在兩點半開始。

questions.text: Students who miss the practical session must arrange a replacement with their tutor.

zh.Students who miss the practical session: 錯過實作課的學生必須與導師安排補課。

questions.text: Reading lists for the second semester are now available on the course website.

zh.Reading lists for the second semester ar: 第二學期的閱讀清單現在已經可以在課程網站上取得。

questions.text: The chemistry laboratory will be closed next week for essential maintenance.

zh.The chemistry laboratory will be closed: 化學實驗室下週將因必要的維修而關閉。

questions.text: Most of the survey participants preferred online classes to traditional lectures.

zh.Most of the survey participants preferre: 大多數受訪者比起傳統講課，更喜歡線上課程。

questions.text: Graduates in engineering often find work before they complete their final exams.

zh.Graduates in engineering often find work: 工程系的畢業生常常在考完期末考之前就找到工作。

questions.text: The committee will announce the scholarship results at the end of the month.

zh.The committee will announce the scholars: 委員會將在月底公布獎學金的結果。

questions.text: Remember to cite every source you use in your written assignments.

zh.Remember to cite every source you use in: 記得在書面作業中註明你使用的每一個資料來源。

questions.text: The history department is organising a field trip to the national museum.

zh.The history department is organising a f: 歷史系正在籌辦一趟前往國家博物館的校外參訪。

questions.text: Group presentations should last no longer than fifteen minutes in total.

zh.Group presentations should last no longe: 小組報告的總時間不應超過十五分鐘。

questions.text: The accommodation office can help international students find suitable housing.

zh.The accommodation office can help intern: 住宿辦公室可以協助國際學生找到合適的住處。

questions.text: Economic growth slowed considerably during the final quarter of the year.

zh.Economic growth slowed considerably duri: 經濟成長在今年最後一季明顯放緩。

questions.text: All first-year students are expected to attend the library induction.

zh.All first-year students are expected to: 所有一年級學生都應參加圖書館的新生導覽。

questions.text: The results of the experiment were published in a leading scientific journal.

zh.The results of the experiment were publi: 這項實驗的結果已發表在一份頂尖的科學期刊上。

questions.text: Please switch off your mobile phones before the examination begins.

zh.Please switch off your mobile phones bef: 考試開始前請關閉你的手機。

questions.text: The library will open two hours later on public holidays.

zh.The library will open two hours later on: 圖書館在國定假日會晚兩個小時開放。

questions.text: Your tutor will give you feedback on the draft within a week.

zh.Your tutor will give you feedback on the: 你的導師會在一週內給你草稿的回饋意見。

questions.text: Several students have asked for the lecture slides to be uploaded earlier.

zh.Several students have asked for the lect: 有好幾位學生要求提早上傳講座的投影片。

questions.text: The field trip has been postponed because of the weather forecast.

zh.The field trip has been postponed becaus: 由於天氣預報的關係，校外考察已經延期。

questions.text: All assignments must be submitted through the online learning system.

zh.All assignments must be submitted throug: 所有作業都必須透過線上學習系統繳交。

questions.text: The professor recommended three books for further reading on the topic.

zh.The professor recommended three books fo: 教授推薦了三本書，作為這個主題的延伸閱讀。

questions.text: Laboratory coats and safety glasses must be worn at all times.

zh.Laboratory coats and safety glasses must: 任何時候都必須穿著實驗衣並戴上護目鏡。

zh.The student union is holding a meeting i: 學生會今晚將在大禮堂舉行會議。

questions.text: Most of the research was carried out in rural parts of the country.

zh.Most of the research was carried out in: 大部分的研究是在這個國家的鄉村地區進行的。

questions.text: The deadline for scholarship applications has been extended by two weeks.

zh.The deadline for scholarship application: 獎學金申請的截止日期已經延後兩週。

zh.Please read the first two chapters befor: 請在下週二的研討課之前讀完前兩章。

questions.text: International students can get advice about visas from the student centre.

zh.International students can get advice ab: 國際學生可以向學生中心諮詢簽證相關事宜。

questions.text: The results suggest that sleep plays an important role in learning.

zh.The results suggest that sleep plays an: 研究結果顯示，睡眠在學習中扮演重要的角色。

questions.caption: Line chart of smartphone ownership among adults aged 18–34 and adults aged 55 and over, 2012 to 2024.
keys: ownership rose in both age groups
18–34s reached near-universal ownership, 97% by 2024
over-55s grew most, from 18% to 80%
the gap narrowed from 48 to 17 percentage points
growth among younger adults levelled off after 2018
questions.model: The line chart shows the percentage of adults owning a smartphone in two age groups between 2012 and 2024. Ownership rose in both groups throughout the period. Among 18 to 34 year olds it climbed from 66 per cent to 92 per cent by 2018 and then levelled off, reaching an almost universal 97 per cent. The over-55s started far lower, at just 18 per cent, but grew much faster, reaching 80 per cent by 2024. As a result, the gap between the two groups narrowed from 48 to 17 percentage points, suggesting that older adults are rapidly catching up.

questions.model: The pie chart illustrates how a university divides its annual budget between five areas. By far the largest share goes on staff salaries, which account for 54 per cent, more than all the other categories put together. Buildings and maintenance take the second largest portion at 16 per cent, followed by research equipment at 12 per cent and student services at 10 per cent. The smallest share, just 8 per cent, is spent on the library and IT. Overall, the chart shows that a university is mainly a people-based organisation, with most of its money spent on the staff who teach and run it.

questions.model: The table compares commuting in five cities by the average one-way journey time and the share of people travelling by public transport or car. Tokyo has the longest commute, at 48 minutes, and also the highest use of public transport, at 57 per cent, while only 12 per cent drive. London follows with 45 minutes and 44 per cent using public transport. In contrast, Toronto and Sydney are car-dependent cities, where 64 and 61 per cent of commuters drive. Berlin has the shortest journey, at just 32 minutes. Overall, the cities with the longest commutes tend to rely most on public transport.

questions.caption: Process diagram showing the five stages of recycling waste paper into new paper.
keys: the process has five stages
paper is first collected and sorted
it is mixed with water and broken down into pulp
ink, glue and other contaminants are removed
the pulp is pressed, dried and rolled into new paper, completing the cycle
questions.model: The diagram shows the five main stages in recycling waste paper. First, used paper is collected and sorted by type. It is then mixed with water and broken down into a soft pulp. In the third stage, ink, glue and other contaminants are removed so that the fibres are clean. After that, the pulp is pressed to squeeze out the water and then dried. Finally, the dried material is rolled into sheets of new paper, which can be sold and eventually recycled again. Overall, the process turns waste into a usable product through a clear sequence of cleaning and reshaping steps.

zh.the pulp is pressed, dried and rolled in: 紙漿經過壓製、乾燥後捲成新紙，完成循環
zh.The diagram shows the five main stages i: 這張圖呈現回收廢紙的五個主要階段。首先，將用過的紙張收集起來並依種類分類。接著把紙與水混合，打碎成柔軟的紙漿。在第三個階段，去除油墨、膠水和其他雜質，使纖維變得乾淨。之後，將紙漿壓製以擠出水分，再加以乾燥。最後，乾燥後的材料被捲成一張張新紙，可以出售，最終也能再次回收。整體而言，這個流程透過一連串清潔和重塑的步驟，把廢棄物變成可用的產品。

keys: the process has five stages
a draft bill is introduced and first debated in parliament
a committee examines it and may suggest amendments
it must be voted on in both houses

questions.model: The diagram shows the five stages by which a proposal becomes law. First, a draft bill is introduced, and it is then debated for the first time in parliament. Next, it is sent to a committee, which examines the details and may suggest amendments. After that, the bill must be approved by a vote in both houses of parliament. Finally, it receives formal approval and becomes law. Overall, the process is designed to give a proposal several rounds of scrutiny before it can take effect.

keys: the water cycle is a continuous loop of five stages
water evaporates from the oceans
the vapour condenses into clouds
it falls as rain or snow
it collects in rivers and lakes and flows back to the sea
questions.model: The diagram illustrates the water cycle, a continuous process with five stages. First, heat from the sun causes water to evaporate from the oceans. As the water vapour rises and cools, it condenses to form clouds. The water then falls back to the ground as precipitation, in the form of rain or snow. After that, it collects in rivers and lakes, and finally it flows back to the sea, where the cycle begins again. Overall, the diagram shows how the same water moves endlessly between the oceans, the atmosphere and the land.

questions.text: Most of us think of a placebo as a trick: it only works if the patient believes they are receiving real medicine. A series of recent trials has challenged that assumption. In so-called open-label studies, patients with chronic back pain or irritable bowel syndrome were handed pills and told plainly that they contained no active ingredient. Remarkably, many still reported meaningful relief compared with patients who received no pills at all. Researchers think the ritual itself matters — taking something regularly, with the attention of a clinician, appears to trigger the body’s own pain-regulating systems. That does not mean placebos can cure disease; they have little effect on tumours or infections. But for conditions where symptoms are shaped by the brain’s interpretation of signals, honesty and effectiveness may not be in conflict after all.

open-label trials told patients the pills were inactive
many still reported relief compared with taking no pills

limits: no effect on tumours or infections, but useful where the brain shapes symptoms

Researchers believe the ritual of treatment and a clinician’s attention trigger the body’s own pain systems. Although placebos cannot cure diseases such as tumours or infections, the lecturer concluded that for symptom-driven conditions, honesty and effectiveness can coexist.

questions.text: The keyboard in front of you is a small lesson in economics. The QWERTY layout was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters, partly to reduce jamming when neighbouring keys were struck in quick succession. The mechanical problem disappeared generations ago, and several alternative layouts claim to be faster. Yet QWERTY has survived, and economists use it as a classic example of path dependence. Once millions of people have learned a system, and manufacturers, schools and employers have organised around it, the cost of switching becomes enormous, even if the alternative is better. Interestingly, later research has questioned how much faster the alternatives really are, which suggests a second lesson: when a standard has lasted this long, it is worth checking whether the story of its inferiority is itself exaggerated.

questions.text: Scattered across parts of the deep ocean floor are potato-sized lumps called polymetallic nodules. They contain nickel, cobalt and manganese, the metals needed for electric vehicle batteries, and several companies are preparing to harvest them with robotic collectors. Supporters argue that mining the seabed could be less damaging than clearing rainforest for mines on land, and that the energy transition depends on these metals. Marine biologists are far more cautious. The nodules grow by only a few millimetres every million years, and they form the only hard surface on which many deep-sea species can live. Studies of test sites disturbed decades ago show that life has still not recovered. The central problem is that we are being asked to approve an industry in an ecosystem we have barely begun to describe.

questions.text: Over the last few years, hundreds of companies have trialled a four-day working week with no reduction in pay. The results have been more positive than many managers expected. In the largest trials, most firms reported that productivity held steady or even improved, while staff reported less burnout and fewer sick days. Recruitment also became easier, because the policy was attractive to job seekers. However, the picture is not uniform. The model works best in office jobs where output can be measured and meetings can be cut. In hospitals, schools and factories, where someone must be present for a fixed number of hours, a shorter week usually means hiring more staff. So the real question is not whether a four-day week works, but in which kinds of work it can pay for itself.

questions.text: Procrastination is often treated as a problem of time management, but psychologists increasingly see it as a problem of emotion regulation. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, delaying it provides immediate relief, even though we know it will cost us later. That short-term reward is why procrastination is so hard to break. Studies of students show that those who procrastinate most are not necessarily lazy or disorganised; they are often the ones most worried about failing. Interestingly, one of the most effective interventions is self-forgiveness. Students who forgave themselves for delaying revision before one exam procrastinated less before the next. The reasoning is that guilt adds another negative emotion to the task, making it even more tempting to avoid. So the solution is less about planners and more about how we treat ourselves when we fall behind.

questions.text: Almost every world map you have seen distorts the planet. It is impossible to flatten a sphere without stretching it somewhere, so every projection involves a compromise. The most famous, the Mercator projection, was designed in 1569 for sailors. Its great advantage is that a straight line on the map is a line of constant compass direction, which made navigation far simpler. The cost is size. Areas far from the equator are enormously enlarged, so Greenland appears roughly the size of Africa, when in reality Africa is about fourteen times larger. Because Mercator maps became the standard in classrooms, generations of students absorbed a distorted sense of the world. Cartographers now argue that the right projection depends on the purpose: Mercator for navigation, and equal-area projections when comparing the sizes of countries.

questions.text: Most of us hate waiting, but research on queues shows that how we feel about a wait depends less on its length than on how it is experienced. Unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, which is why lifts have mirrors and theme parks entertain people in line. Uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, so a display saying fifteen minutes makes a wait more tolerable. Perhaps most importantly, unfair waits feel longer than fair ones. People become far more upset when someone who arrived later is served first. This is why a single queue feeding several counters, although not faster on average, is usually preferred to separate lines. For businesses, the lesson is that improving the experience of waiting can matter as much as reducing it.

questions.text: When we talk about coastal flooding, we usually focus on rising seas. But in many of the world’s largest coastal cities, the land itself is sinking, often faster than the sea is rising. The main cause is groundwater extraction. When water is pumped out of the layers of clay and sand beneath a city, those layers compact, and the surface drops. Parts of Jakarta have sunk by more than four metres over recent decades. The encouraging news is that subsidence can be slowed. Tokyo sank rapidly in the mid-twentieth century, but after strict limits were placed on groundwater pumping and the city switched to piped water from rivers, the sinking almost stopped. The lesson is that, unlike sea level rise, subsidence is largely a local problem with local solutions.

questions.text: Fermentation is one of the oldest food technologies we have. Long before anyone understood microbes, people discovered that leaving certain foods under the right conditions made them last longer and taste different. Bread, cheese, yoghurt, soy sauce and kimchi all depend on bacteria or yeasts transforming sugars into acids, gases or alcohol. The finished products are more acidic or salty than the raw ingredients, which stops harmful organisms from growing. In recent years, fermented foods have attracted attention for another reason: their possible effect on the gut. Some small trials suggest that eating them regularly increases the diversity of gut bacteria and reduces markers of inflammation. However, the evidence is still limited, and it is worth remembering that many shop-bought products are pasteurised, which kills the living cultures that may provide the benefit.

questions.text: We often talk about data travelling through the cloud, but almost all international internet traffic actually travels through cables on the sea floor. There are more than four hundred of them, some stretching over twenty thousand kilometres. Each is only about the thickness of a garden hose, with glass fibres carrying signals as pulses of light. Satellites carry a surprisingly small share of traffic, because cables are far cheaper per unit of data and much faster. The main threat to these cables is not sabotage but accidents: ships’ anchors and fishing trawlers cause most of the roughly one hundred and fifty faults each year. Repairs are handled by a small fleet of specialised ships, and because so many countries depend on a few routes, a single break can slow the internet for an entire region.

many countries rely on a few routes, so one break can slow a whole region

questions.text: One of the most striking findings in behavioural economics concerns organ donation. In some European countries, fewer than twenty per cent of people are registered donors, while in neighbouring countries with similar cultures the figure is above ninety per cent. The difference is not attitudes but defaults. Where people must opt in to become donors, most never get round to it. Where they are donors unless they opt out, most never opt out. Defaults work because they require no effort, and because people often interpret them as a recommendation. However, higher registration does not automatically mean more transplants, since families are usually consulted and hospitals need the capacity to act. So defaults are a powerful tool, but only one part of a system that has to work as a whole.

questions.title: Should first-year exams be abolished?

turns.text: I think first-year exams should go. The first year is about adjusting to university, and high-stakes exams just push students into cramming. Continuous assessment — short essays, lab reports, quizzes — gives a far better picture of what someone can actually do.

The trouble with continuous assessment is that it’s much easier to get help with. An essay can be polished by a friend, or these days by software. An exam is the one situation where we know the work is the student’s own.

Both of those are true, but you’re treating it as all or nothing. The research on first-year retention suggests students drop out when they fail something big early and feel they don’t belong. The problem isn’t exams as such, it’s one exam deciding everything.
So you’d keep exams but lower the weight?
Exactly. Keep a supervised exam for integrity, but make it worth, say, thirty per cent, and let the rest come from work spread across the year.
I could live with that, as long as the exam still has to be passed on its own. Otherwise people will ignore it completely.

questions.title: Should the city centre be closed to cars?

turns.text: Our city centre is choked with traffic, and the air quality readings on the high street are the worst in the region. Cities like Oslo and Ghent closed their centres to private cars and footfall actually went up. I think we should do the same.

I run a shop there, so I’m wary. Those cities had excellent public transport before the ban. Here, the buses stop at seven in the evening. If you close the centre tomorrow, my older customers simply won’t come.

I think the sequence is what matters. The evidence from Ghent is that they redesigned the bus network first and phased the restrictions in over two years. Doing it the other way round is how you get a backlash.
Fair enough. So start with the buses and delivery hours, then close streets gradually?
And keep access for disabled drivers and deliveries in the mornings. With that, I would support it.
And we should measure footfall and air quality before and after, so the decision rests on local data, not just examples from abroad.

Fatima: as a shop owner, fears losing older customers because buses stop at 7 pm
Chen: sequence matters; Ghent improved buses first and phased restrictions in over two years
agreement: improve buses first, close streets gradually, keep access for disabled drivers and morning deliveries
Chen: measure footfall and air quality before and after

Chen argued that the order of changes matters, as Ghent improved its buses before phasing in restrictions. They agreed to upgrade buses first, close streets gradually and keep access for disabled drivers and deliveries, while Chen added that footfall and air quality should be measured.

questions.title: AI tools and university assignments

turns.text: I use AI tools to brainstorm before I start an essay. They’re good at suggesting angles I wouldn’t have thought of, and I still write every sentence myself. Banning them feels like banning calculators.

The calculator comparison doesn’t really work, though. A calculator gives you a correct answer to a question you already understand. These tools can produce a plausible essay on a topic you don’t understand at all, and the marker can’t tell the difference.

I think we’re arguing about the wrong thing. Whether it’s allowed matters less than whether the assessment still measures learning. If an assignment can be completed entirely by a chatbot, the assignment is badly designed.
That’s convenient for students, but it puts the whole burden on lecturers to redesign everything overnight.
Not overnight. But more in-class writing, oral defences of essays, and asking students to show their drafts would all help.
And being honest about it. If each course said clearly what use is allowed, most students would follow the rules.

keys: Ruby: uses AI to brainstorm but writes every sentence herself; a ban would be like banning calculators
Marcus: the comparison fails, because AI can write plausible essays on topics students don’t understand
Aisha: the real question is whether assessment still measures learning; tasks a chatbot can complete are badly designed
Marcus: this puts the burden on lecturers
solutions: in-class writing, oral defences and drafts, plus clear rules on allowed use (Ruby)
questions.model: The group discussed AI tools in university assignments. Ruby said she uses AI only to brainstorm and compared a ban to banning calculators. Marcus rejected the comparison, arguing that AI can produce convincing essays on topics students do not understand, which markers cannot detect. They suggested in-class writing, oral defences and draft submission, and Ruby added that courses should state clearly what use is allowed.

questions.title: A plant-based menu for the campus canteen?

turns.text: The sustainability committee wants the main canteen to go fully plant-based. Food is about a quarter of our campus emissions, and beef alone accounts for most of that. It’s the single biggest change we could make quickly.
I agree on the emissions, but a full switch removes choice, and I suspect students would just buy burgers off campus instead. Then emissions don’t fall; they just move somewhere we can’t see them.
There’s decent evidence on how to avoid that. Universities that made plant-based dishes the default, cheaper and placed first, saw meat sales fall by about a third without banning anything.
A third is good, but it’s not the same as eliminating beef.
No, but you could remove beef specifically, since it has by far the highest footprint, and keep chicken and fish on the menu.
That I could support. Drop beef, make the plant-based option the cheaper default, and publish the emissions figures each term so we can see if it works.

Kwame: making plant-based dishes the cheaper default cut meat sales by about a third
compromise: remove beef, but keep chicken and fish
plant-based as the cheaper default, with emissions published each term (Isabel)

questions.title: Should the library open 24 hours?

turns.text: I think the library should stay open all night during exam periods. Lots of students work part-time or care for family during the day, and the evening is the only quiet time they get. Right now it closes at ten, just when some of us are getting started.
I understand that, but staffing a building all night is expensive, and the university says the money would come out of the book budget. I’d rather have the resources than the extra hours.

There’s also a wellbeing question. Some universities that tried twenty-four-hour opening found that a small group of students were basically living there and not sleeping. I’m not sure we want to encourage that.
That’s fair, but banning access doesn’t make people sleep. They just work somewhere worse.
What if only one floor stayed open overnight, with security rather than library staff? That would cost far less.
And limit it to the four weeks around exams. Then we could see how many people actually use it before deciding whether to make it permanent.

questions.title: Is a gap year worthwhile?

turns.text: I took a gap year before university and it was the best decision I made. I worked for six months, then volunteered abroad, and I arrived at university knowing what I wanted to study and why.

That worked for you, but a gap year assumes you can afford one. Travelling and volunteering abroad is expensive, and for many students the real choice is between starting their degree or starting work.

I think the useful part isn’t the travel at all. The research I’ve seen suggests students who take a year out do slightly better at university, but mainly because they’ve had time to mature and choose a course carefully.
That’s true — the six months of work taught me more than the volunteering, honestly.
Then universities could offer deferred places more easily, so that students can work locally for a year without losing their offer.
Exactly. A structured year of paid work, with the place held for you, gets the benefits without the cost.

Sophie argued that the benefit comes from maturity and careful course choice rather than travel, and Emma agreed that working taught her more. They concluded that universities should make deferred places easier, allowing students to spend a year in paid local work without losing their offer.

questions.title: Should the city pay for a new stadium?

turns.text: I think the council should help fund the new stadium. It would bring major events to the city, create jobs during construction, and give the area around the old railway yard a reason to be regenerated.

The evidence on that is actually quite poor. Studies of publicly funded stadiums in many countries find little lasting economic benefit. Most of the spending on match days is money local people would have spent in the city anyway, just on something else.
I agree the economic case is weak, but I don’t think that’s the only question. A stadium can also matter for civic identity. The issue is who takes the risk if it loses money.
So you’d support it if the club carried the risk?
Largely, yes. The council could provide the land and transport links, which benefit everyone, while the club pays for the building itself.
I could accept that, as long as the council doesn’t guarantee the club’s loans. That’s where cities usually get burned.

Priyanka: studies find little lasting economic benefit, as spending is mostly displaced
Liam: stadiums matter for civic identity, but the key question is who carries the risk
proposal: the council provides land and transport, the club pays for the building
Priyanka agrees if the council does not guarantee the club’s loans

They agreed the council could provide land and transport while the club funds the building, provided the council does not guarantee the club’s loans.

questions.title: Should restaurants add a service charge?

turns.text: I’d like restaurants to add a fixed service charge instead of relying on tips. Tipping makes staff income unpredictable, and research shows tips depend more on the customer’s mood and the server’s appearance than on the quality of service.
But a fixed charge removes the customer’s choice. If the service is poor, a tip is the only way I can show it. And some restaurants keep part of the service charge rather than passing it to staff.
In my country there’s no tipping at all — prices simply include fair wages. Service is excellent, because staff are trained and paid properly, not because they’re chasing tips.
So maybe the real solution isn’t a service charge but higher wages built into the menu prices.
I could accept that, if menu prices are clear and there’s no extra charge added at the end. What annoys people is surprises on the bill.
And any service charge that remains should go to staff by law, so customers know where their money is going.

questions.title: Should social media be restricted for under-16s?

turns.text: I support a legal minimum age of sixteen for social media. Rates of anxiety among teenagers have risen sharply since smartphones became common, and the platforms are designed to keep young people scrolling.

The timing is suggestive, but the research linking social media to teenage anxiety is actually quite mixed. Most studies find small average effects. And for some young people, especially those who feel isolated, online communities are a real lifeline.

I think we’re focusing on the wrong thing. A ban is almost impossible to enforce without checking everyone’s identity online. The design features are the problem — endless feeds, notifications at night, recommendation systems.
So you’d regulate the design rather than the age?
Yes. For example, no notifications overnight and no endless scrolling for younger users.
I’d support that, as long as young people can still reach support groups. And schools should teach how these platforms are designed to capture attention.

questions.title: Group projects: one mark or individual marks?

turns.text: I think group projects should give everyone the same mark. The whole point is learning to work as a team, and if marks are individual, people stop helping each other and just protect their own section.
But that’s exactly why shared marks feel unfair. In my last project, one person did almost nothing and got the same grade as the rest of us. It punishes the students who carry the work.
Some courses use peer assessment to deal with that. Each member rates the others’ contribution, and the group mark is adjusted up or down for each person.
Doesn’t that just turn into people voting for their friends?
It can, which is why the ratings need to be backed up by evidence, like meeting notes and a record of who did which task.
That would work for me. Keep one group mark, but let it be adjusted when there’s clear evidence that someone didn’t contribute.

questions.title: Should the campus ban plastic water bottles?

turns.text: I’d like the campus shops to stop selling bottled water altogether. Thousands of plastic bottles are thrown away here every week, and most of them are never recycled.

The problem is that some universities that banned bottled water saw sales of sugary drinks in plastic bottles go up. People still wanted something to drink on the go, so the plastic didn’t disappear, it just changed shape.

That’s the key point, I think. A ban only works if there’s a convenient alternative. At the moment there are only three water fountains on the whole campus, and one of them has been broken since September.
So we fix the fountains first?
Fix them and add refill stations in every building, and maybe give new students a free reusable bottle at enrolment.
Then phase out bottled water once the stations are in place, and track sales of other bottled drinks, so we know the plastic is actually going down.

zh.agree practical next steps or support: 商定實際可行的下一步或支援方式
zh.confirm what is expected for the next de: 確認下一個截止期限的要求
zh.Thanks for making time, Sam. I wanted to: Sam，謝謝你抽出時間。我想私下跟你談談，因為你平常是團隊裡最可靠的人之一，但這個月有兩個期限延誤了——客戶報告和預算摘要。我不是來批評你的，只是想了解發生了什麼事。目前是不是有什麼事情讓工作量變得吃力，不管是工作上還是工作以外的？如果是專案太多的問題，我們可以考慮把其中一個轉給別人。我確實需要下一份報告在十五號之前完成，所以我們現在就來談談，怎麼做才能讓這個目標實際可行。

questions.text: You ordered a laptop online, but it arrived with a cracked screen. You call the company’s customer service line. What do you say?
keys: identify yourself and the order clearly
describe the damage precisely
say when it arrived and that it was damaged on delivery
state the outcome you want: a replacement or a refund
ask about the next steps and how long they will take
questions.model: Hello, I’m calling about an order I received yesterday. The order number is 48213, and it was a fourteen-inch laptop. When I opened the box, the screen was cracked across the bottom left corner, so it must have been damaged before it reached me — the packaging was dented as well. I have taken photos of both the screen and the box. I would like a replacement sent out as soon as possible, or a full refund if that model is out of stock. Could you tell me how to return the damaged one and how long the replacement will take?

zh.Hello, I’m calling about an order I rece: 你好，我打來是想詢問我昨天收到的一筆訂單。訂單編號是 48213，是一台十四吋的筆記型電腦。我打開箱子時，螢幕左下角有一道裂痕，所以一定是在送到我手上之前就已經損壞了——包裝也有凹痕。我已經把螢幕和箱子都拍了照片。我希望你們盡快寄一台新的給我，如果那個型號缺貨，就請全額退款。可以請你告訴我要怎麼退回損壞的那台，以及換貨需要多久時間嗎？

questions.text: A friend has invited you to her birthday dinner on Saturday, but you have already agreed to work an extra shift that evening. You call her. What do you say?

explain honestly why you cannot come
apologise and show that you are disappointed
suggest another way to celebrate together
end on a warm, positive note

Unfortunately, I have already agreed to cover an extra shift at work on Saturday evening, and I can’t get out of it now because they are short of staff. I’m really sorry, because I would have loved to be there. Could I take you out for lunch next week instead, just the two of us? My treat, to make up for it. I hope you have a wonderful evening, and happy birthday in advance!

zh.A friend has invited you to her birthday: 一位朋友邀請你星期六參加她的生日晚餐，但你已經答應那天晚上要多值一個班。你打電話給她。你會怎麼說？
zh.explain honestly why you cannot come: 誠實說明你無法出席的原因

zh.Hi Mia, thank you so much for the invita: 嗨，Mia，非常謝謝妳的邀請——妳有想到我，對我來說真的意義重大。可惜的是，我已經答應星期六晚上要幫忙多值一個班，而且因為他們人手不足，我現在沒辦法推掉。真的很抱歉，因為我很想去參加。下週我請妳吃午餐好嗎？就我們兩個人。我請客，算是補償。祝妳有個美好的夜晚，也先祝妳生日快樂！

explain the mistake clearly: what you ordered and what arrived
mention that you are short of time
ask for a practical solution, such as a quick replacement or takeaway

Would it be possible to get the salad quickly, or if that will take a while, could I have it to take away? Thank you so much, I really appreciate your help.

zh.You are at a café and the waiter has bro: 你在一家咖啡廳，服務生送錯了餐點。你很趕時間，因為十五分鐘後就要上課了。你會對服務生說什麼？

show that you have read the feedback carefully
identify the specific section you think was misread

ask how to improve next time

It says the argument was missing a counter-view, but I did try to address that in the second paragraph of that section. Could you have another look at it, or explain what I should have done differently? Either way, I’d really like to understand how to improve for the next assignment.

zh.show that you have read the feedback car: 表現出你已經仔細讀過回饋意見

questions.text: You are organising a study group, but one member keeps arriving late and the others are becoming frustrated. You speak to him after the session. What do you say?

describe the lateness and its effect on the group
ask whether something is causing it

If so, we could move it to later in the afternoon. If not, could you try to be here by four? We really value what you bring to the group, so I’d rather sort this out than have people drift away.

explain when it came on and what you did
reassure your friend that you drove carefully
offer to help, for example by taking it to a garage or paying for a check

On Sunday afternoon an orange warning light came on, the one that looks like an engine. I pulled over and checked the manual, and it said it was safe to drive gently, so I came straight back without going on the motorway. I don’t know whether it was something I did, but I’d be happy to take it to a garage this week and cover the cost of the check. I just didn’t want you to find out on your own.

zh.You borrowed a friend’s car for the week: 你週末向朋友借了車，開車時儀表板亮起了一個警示燈。你現在要把車還給朋友。你會怎麼說？
