zh.Correct. “There are also costs for the a: 正確。"There are also costs for the animals that succeed"，例如更高音調的鳴唱和受干擾的繁殖。

questions.passage: Public fear of nuclear power is closely linked to a small number of dramatic accidents, especially Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011. Yet when researchers compare energy sources by the number of deaths per unit of electricity produced, including accidents and air pollution, nuclear power ranks among the safest, alongside wind and solar. Coal is by far the most dangerous, mainly because the pollution from burning it contributes to heart and lung disease. At Fukushima, the radiation itself is thought to have caused very few deaths; most of the lives lost were connected to the stress and disruption of a rushed evacuation, particularly among elderly people. None of this means nuclear power is free of problems. Plants are expensive and slow to build, and the long-term storage of radioactive waste remains politically difficult in most countries. But researchers argue that decisions about energy should be based on the full comparison of risks, rather than on the vividness of rare disasters.
questions.q: Which statements are supported by the passage?
o: Measured by deaths per unit of electricity, nuclear power is among the safest sources.
Coal is the most dangerous source mainly because of mining accidents.
Most deaths linked to Fukushima were related to the evacuation rather than radiation.
Nuclear plants are cheap and quick to build.
Radioactive waste storage has been fully solved in most countries.
why: Correct. By deaths per unit of electricity, “nuclear power ranks among the safest, alongside wind and solar”.
Wrong. Coal is most dangerous “mainly because the pollution from burning it contributes to heart and lung disease”, not because of mining accidents.
Correct. “most of the lives lost were connected to the stress and disruption of a rushed evacuation”.
Wrong. “Plants are expensive and slow to build.”
Wrong. Waste storage “remains politically difficult in most countries”.

zh.Public fear of nuclear power is closely: 大眾對核能的恐懼，與少數幾起戲劇性的事故密切相關，尤其是 1986 年的車諾比和 2011 年的福島。然而，當研究人員以每單位發電量的死亡人數來比較各種能源時，把事故和空氣污染都算進去，核能與風力、太陽能並列為最安全的能源之一。煤炭遠遠是最危險的，主要是因為燃燒煤炭產生的污染會導致心臟和肺部疾病。在福島，一般認為輻射本身造成的死亡人數非常少；大部分的死亡與倉促疏散所帶來的壓力和混亂有關，尤其是在年長者之中。這並不表示核能沒有問題。核電廠的興建成本高昂且耗時，而放射性廢料的長期儲存在大多數國家仍然是政治上的難題。但研究人員認為，能源政策應該根據全面的風險比較來決定，而不是根據罕見災難給人的鮮明印象。

questions.passage: Kelp forests are underwater forests of large brown algae that grow in cool, nutrient-rich coastal waters. Some kelp species can grow up to half a metre in a single day, making them among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth. The forests provide food and shelter for hundreds of species, from fish to sea otters. Sea otters in turn protect the kelp by eating sea urchins, which would otherwise graze the forests down to bare rock. When otters were hunted almost to extinction for their fur, urchin populations exploded along parts of the Pacific coast, and large areas of kelp disappeared. More recently, marine heatwaves have caused dramatic losses, since kelp struggles in warm water. Restoration projects are now removing urchins by hand and replanting kelp, with some success. Kelp is also attracting commercial interest as a food, a fertiliser and a possible way of storing carbon, although how much of that carbon is stored permanently is still debated.
questions.q: Which of the following are stated or implied in the passage?
o: Sea otters damage kelp forests by feeding on them.
The decline of sea otters led to kelp losses in some areas.
Marine heatwaves have harmed kelp forests.
Scientists agree that kelp stores large amounts of carbon permanently.
why: Correct. Some species “can grow up to half a metre in a single day”.
Wrong. Otters “protect the kelp by eating sea urchins”; it is the urchins that graze the forests.
Correct. When otters were hunted, “urchin populations exploded … and large areas of kelp disappeared”.
Correct. “marine heatwaves have caused dramatic losses, since kelp struggles in warm water”.
Wrong. “how much of that carbon is stored permanently is still debated”.

zh.Kelp forests are underwater forests of l: 海藻林是由大型褐藻組成的水下森林，生長在涼爽且營養豐富的沿海水域。有些海帶品種一天之內可以長高半公尺，是地球上生長最快的生物之一。這些森林為數百種物種提供食物和棲身之處，從魚類到海獺都有。海獺則反過來透過吃海膽來保護海藻，否則海膽會把森林啃食到只剩光禿禿的岩石。當海獺因為毛皮而被獵捕到幾乎滅絕時，太平洋沿岸部分地區的海膽數量暴增，大片的海藻因此消失。近來，海洋熱浪造成了劇烈的損失，因為海藻在溫暖的水中難以生存。復育計畫目前正以人工方式移除海膽並重新種植海藻，取得了一些成效。海藻作為食物、肥料以及可能的碳儲存方式，也引起了商業上的興趣，不過其中有多少碳能被永久儲存，至今仍有爭議。

questions.passage: The fork is such an ordinary object that it is easy to forget how recently it became common. Although small forks were used in the ancient world for serving food, eating with a personal fork spread into Europe from the Byzantine Empire only around the eleventh century. Early reactions were often hostile. Church leaders criticised the fork as an unnecessary luxury, arguing that fingers were good enough for the food God had provided. For several centuries, Europeans continued to eat mainly with knives, spoons and their hands, and the fork was associated with the Italian upper classes. It became common in England only in the eighteenth century, and early forks had just two straight prongs, which were better for holding meat steady while cutting than for lifting food. The curved, four-pronged fork familiar today developed later, as eating habits changed. In much of East Asia, meanwhile, chopsticks had been in everyday use for well over two thousand years.
questions.q: Which of the following are stated in the passage?
o: Personal forks reached Europe from the Byzantine Empire.
Church leaders encouraged forks as a sign of good manners.
Forks became common in England in the eighteenth century.
Early forks usually had four curved prongs.
Chopsticks were in use in East Asia long before forks were common in Europe.
why: Correct. Eating with a personal fork “spread into Europe from the Byzantine Empire only around the eleventh century”.
Wrong. Church leaders “criticised the fork as an unnecessary luxury”.
Correct. “It became common in England only in the eighteenth century.”
Wrong. “early forks had just two straight prongs”; the curved, four-pronged fork “developed later”.
Correct. Chopsticks “had been in everyday use for well over two thousand years”.

zh.The fork is such an ordinary object that: 叉子是如此平凡的物品，以至於人們很容易忘記它其實是最近才普及的。雖然古代世界就有用來盛裝食物的小叉子，但用個人專屬的叉子進食，大約到十一世紀才從拜占庭帝國傳入歐洲。早期的反應往往是敵視的。教會領袖批評叉子是一種不必要的奢侈品，認為用手指來吃上帝賜予的食物就夠了。在好幾個世紀裡，歐洲人仍然主要用刀子、湯匙和雙手進食，而叉子則與義大利的上流階層聯想在一起。叉子直到十八世紀才在英國普及，而早期的叉子只有兩根直齒，比較適合在切肉時把肉固定住，而不是用來把食物送進嘴裡。今天大家熟悉的彎曲四齒叉，是後來隨著飲食習慣改變才發展出來的。與此同時，在東亞大部分地區，筷子早已在日常生活中使用了兩千多年。

questions.passage: Gamification, the use of game features such as points, badges and leaderboards in non-game settings, has become popular in education. Supporters argue that it makes learning more engaging, particularly for students who struggle with motivation. Research gives a mixed picture. Many studies report short-term increases in participation, especially when students receive frequent feedback on their progress. However, these gains often fade once the novelty wears off, and some studies find that leaderboards discourage lower-performing students, who see themselves permanently near the bottom. Psychologists also warn that external rewards can weaken interest in an activity that students already enjoy, a phenomenon known as the overjustification effect. The most successful designs appear to be those that use game elements to support learning goals rather than replace them, for example by giving students clear, achievable challenges and letting them see their own improvement over time rather than comparing them with classmates.
questions.q: Which of the following are supported by the passage?
o: Gamification often increases participation in the short term.
The benefits of gamification usually grow stronger over time.
Leaderboards can discourage students who rank low.
External rewards can reduce interest in activities students already enjoy.
The best designs compare each student’s progress with that of their classmates.
why: Correct. “Many studies report short-term increases in participation.”
Wrong. “these gains often fade once the novelty wears off”.
Correct. “leaderboards discourage lower-performing students, who see themselves permanently near the bottom”.
Correct. “external rewards can weaken interest in an activity that students already enjoy”, the overjustification effect.
Wrong. The best designs let students see “their own improvement over time rather than comparing them with classmates”.

questions.passage: Historians and scientists have increasingly identified the year 536 as one of the worst times to be alive in recorded history. Writers in Europe and the Middle East described a mysterious fog that dimmed the sun for more than a year, and summer temperatures in parts of the northern hemisphere fell sharply. Tree rings from this period show some of the slowest growth ever recorded, and chronicles report failed harvests and famine in regions as far apart as Ireland and China. For a long time the cause was unknown. Analysis of ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica has now revealed evidence of a major volcanic eruption early in 536, followed by further eruptions in 540 and 547, which together kept temperatures low for over a decade. Some researchers link the resulting hardship to the spread of plague a few years later, arguing that populations weakened by hunger were more vulnerable, although that connection remains difficult to prove.
questions.q: Which of the following can be concluded from the passage?
o: Summer temperatures fell in parts of the northern hemisphere in 536.
The cause of the cold period is still completely unknown.
Tree rings provide evidence of poor growing conditions at that time.
A single eruption was responsible for the whole cold decade.
The link between the cold years and plague has been firmly proven.
why: Correct. “summer temperatures in parts of the northern hemisphere fell sharply”.
Wrong. The cause was unknown “for a long time”, but ice cores “now” reveal volcanic eruptions.
Correct. “Tree rings from this period show some of the slowest growth ever recorded.”
Wrong. There were further eruptions “in 540 and 547, which together kept temperatures low”.
Wrong. That connection “remains difficult to prove”.

zh.Wrong. That connection “remains difficul: 錯誤。這個關聯 "remains difficult to prove"。

order: In 1928 Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mould growing on one of his bacterial cultures.
Around the mould, he noticed, the bacteria had been killed, leaving a clear ring on the dish.
He named the active substance penicillin, but he struggled to produce it in useful quantities.
More than a decade later, a team at Oxford developed methods to purify it and tested it on patients.
Mass production followed during the Second World War, and antibiotics soon transformed medicine.
why: The opener. It gives a date and introduces Fleming and the mould without referring back to anything.
“Around the mould” needs the mould to have been mentioned already, and “he noticed” continues Fleming’s discovery.
“the active substance” is whatever killed the bacteria in the previous sentence; naming it follows observing its effect.
“More than a decade later” follows the problem of producing it, and the Oxford team solves that problem.
The closer. Mass production is the last step, and “soon transformed medicine” sums up the whole story.

order: The Dead Sea, on the border between Jordan and Israel, is one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth.

“As a result” needs a cause, and the diversion of the river is that cause.
The closer. “The retreating shoreline” is the consequence of the falling surface just described.

order: For most of history, people could travel between countries without any official document at all.
This changed during the First World War, when governments introduced passports to control who crossed their borders.
The measure was meant to be temporary, but it outlasted the war that had created it.
In 1920 an international conference agreed on a standard format: a booklet with a photograph and a description of the holder.
That design, updated with electronic chips, is still the basis of the passport in your pocket today.
why: The opener. It describes the general situation “for most of history” and refers back to nothing.
“This changed” needs a situation to change: the travel without documents just described.
“The measure” refers to the passports introduced in the previous sentence, and “the war” to the First World War.

The closer. “That design” points back to the 1920 booklet and brings the story up to the present.

order: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass.
He pointed to the way the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces.
Most geologists rejected the idea, because Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents.
That explanation arrived in the 1960s, when maps of the ocean floor revealed spreading ridges.
Continental drift, once dismissed, became the foundation of modern geology as plate tectonics.

“the idea” refers back to Wegener’s proposal, and the missing force sets up what comes next.
“That explanation” answers exactly what Wegener “could not explain”.
The closer. “once dismissed” looks back over the whole story and gives its outcome.

zh.Continental drift, once dismissed, becam: 曾經被摒棄的大陸漂移說，以「板塊構造論」的形式成為現代地質學的基礎。——結尾句。"once dismissed" 回顧了整個故事並給出結果。

order: The idea of a tunnel beneath the English Channel was first proposed in 1802 by a French engineer.
Over the following century, several attempts began but were abandoned, largely because of British fears of invasion.
It was not until 1988 that construction of the modern tunnel finally started.
Teams from both countries dug towards each other and met beneath the sea in 1990.
The tunnel opened to passengers in 1994, almost two hundred years after it was first imagined.
why: The opener. It introduces the tunnel in full with the earliest date, 1802.
“Over the following century” needs a starting point, the 1802 proposal, and explains why early attempts failed.
“It was not until 1988” marks the end of the long delay just described and the start of real construction.
Digging and meeting in 1990 follows the start of construction in 1988.
The closer. Opening in 1994 is the final event, and “first imagined” links back to the opener.

order: Before a new vaccine can be approved, it must pass through several stages of testing.
It is first given to a small group of healthy volunteers to check that it is safe.
If no serious side effects appear, a larger trial examines the best dose and the immune response.
Finally, thousands of people take part in a trial comparing the vaccine with a placebo.
Only when this final stage shows clear protection do regulators consider granting approval.
why: The opener. It introduces “a new vaccine” and announces the stages that the rest of the paragraph describes.
“It is first given” refers back to the vaccine and begins the sequence of stages.
“If no serious side effects appear” depends on the safety check in the previous stage.
“Finally” marks the last testing stage, which follows the dose trial.
The closer. “this final stage” refers back to the large trial, and approval ends the process.
